title: Observe the task in context
outcome: Record what a patient does, what the service does, and what remains to investigate.
context: The clinic team watches six fictional check-in sessions during a busy morning and records kiosk and reception events.
teach: Observation starts with a person's task in its real setting. Record the starting goal, visible actions, system responses, interruptions, and what happens next. A field note gains value through sequence and context: Mira entered a code, read the screen, walked to reception, and asked whether she had checked in.

Give each note a clear evidence label. An observation records an action or event the researcher saw. A participant report records the person's own account. An interpretation proposes a reason for the action. These three forms of evidence can sit beside one another while keeping their different strengths clear.

Time and environment matter. A queue refresh may happen after the kiosk receipt; a patient may step away to read a sign; an announcement may interrupt a spoken instruction. Record the timing and setting when they could explain the behavior. Follow-up questions can ask what the patient expected at a specific moment.

A small set of sessions helps reveal a possible failure mechanism. The team can then check logs, speak with staff, and observe further sessions to learn how widely that mechanism appears. The first output is a faithful account of the task and a focused list of questions.
keyDistinction: A field note separates visible behavior, participant explanation, and researcher interpretation.
workedExample: A researcher writes: '09:14:02 Mira pressed Check in. The screen showed Done. At 09:14:24 she asked reception whether her arrival was recorded. Mira said she expected her name to appear on the staff screen.' The first three sentences report events and Mira's words. The researcher adds a separate interpretation: the Done message may leave the staff handoff unclear. A queue log can help test that interpretation.
guidedQuestion: Which note gives the team the clearest starting account of Mira's session?

options.label: Mira looked confused by the Done screen and asked reception for help.
options.feedback: This captures a possible interpretation and her help request. Add the visible actions and Mira's own words so colleagues can examine the same evidence.

options.label: Mira pressed Check in, saw Done, and asked reception whether her arrival was recorded.
options.feedback: This preserves a useful sequence. Add the time, surrounding conditions, and Mira's explanation in separate lines for a richer field note.

options.label: At 09:14 Mira pressed Check in; Done appeared; she then asked reception whether her arrival was recorded.
options.feedback: This keeps the sequence and question close to observable evidence. Record Mira's own explanation separately and connect the note to the queue timing.

evidenceShift: A recording that shows Mira reacting to a nearby sign can add the sign to the sequence and guide the next research question.
transferContext: At 09:18 another patient reads the kiosk receipt, walks to the waiting area, and returns to reception after an announcement names a different patient.
transferTask: Write three observation notes, one participant question, and one tentative interpretation from the supplied events. Label each line.
evidencePacket: Fictional observation: at 09:18:10 the patient reads the kiosk receipt and walks to the waiting area.
Fictional observation: at 09:19:05 an announcement names a different patient; the patient returns to reception.
Fictional participant report: 'I thought I might have missed my name.'
artifact: A structured field note with event times, evidence labels, and a next question.
assessmentFocus: The note preserves the order of events and gives each observation, report, and interpretation its own label.
assessmentCriteria: The patient's words appear as a participant report.
The next question follows from the recorded sequence.

title: Choose evidence for the decision
outcome: Match each research question to a method and its limits.
context: Several patients ask reception whether the kiosk recorded their arrival. The team wants to decide what to improve first.
teach: Start with a decision the team faces. Here the decision is whether to change the kiosk message, the staff queue, or both. Turn that decision into questions: when does the appointment service accept an arrival, when does reception see it, and what do patients understand from the message? Each question points toward a different source of evidence.

System logs can establish request and receipt timing. Queue records can show when a receipt becomes visible to staff. Observation can show how a patient uses the kiosk and seeks help. Interviews can reveal the patient's expectation and the meaning they gave to the message. Support notes can expose recurring situations that deserve closer study.

Every source has a useful boundary. A log records system events; the patient's interpretation comes from observing and speaking with the patient. A small observation study reveals behaviors and possible causes; broader service data helps estimate frequency. Combining sources helps the team check whether one explanation fits the whole task.

Write a compact evidence plan with the question, source, expected signal, and limit for each row. Collect the evidence that would change the decision. This focus keeps research connected to a practical improvement.
keyDistinction: Evidence becomes useful when its source and its limits match a specific decision question.
workedExample: The team sees a rise in reception questions after kiosk check-in. A researcher pairs three checks: appointment logs for receipt timing, queue records for staff visibility, and short task observations for patient interpretation. The logs show receipts within three seconds and queue updates up to 90 seconds later. Observation then reveals whether the Done message leads patients to expect an immediate staff display.
guidedQuestion: The team needs to decide whether the first change belongs in kiosk status copy or the staff queue. Which evidence plan gives them the clearest comparison?

options.label: Interview patients about the Done message and prepare new kiosk wording.
options.feedback: Interviews can reveal expectations and language. Pair them with receipt and queue timing to locate the handoff that the wording needs to describe.

options.label: Compare receipt and queue timestamps, observe check-in tasks, and ask patients what each status means.
options.feedback: This combines system events with patient interpretation. The plan can distinguish a delayed queue from an unclear status and guide a targeted first change.

options.label: Count reception questions each day and redesign the queue when the count rises.
options.feedback: A daily count helps track demand. Add task observations and system timing so the redesign addresses the mechanism behind the questions.

evidenceShift: A queue that updates immediately would focus the next study on the message, environment, and patient's understanding of completion.
transferContext: The clinic also records patients who begin check-in and later complete it with reception staff.
transferTask: Choose one question about this channel switch and pair it with two evidence sources. State what each source can establish and what you would examine next.
evidencePacket: Fictional log detail: appointment-service receipts usually arrive within three seconds.
Fictional operations detail: the staff queue can refresh up to 90 seconds later.
Fictional service data: reception tracks requests for check-in help by day, with a free-text note for each request.
artifact: A question-to-evidence matrix with source, expected signal, limitation, and decision consequence.
assessmentFocus: The plan connects a practical decision to multiple complementary sources and states the limits of each.
assessmentCriteria: The decision appears before the method choices.
Each source answers a named question.
The plan distinguishes system timing from patient interpretation.

title: Separate the symptom from its causes
outcome: Compare plausible explanations and choose evidence that separates them.
context: Mira asks reception whether her check-in worked after the kiosk displays Done.
teach: A symptom is the event the team wants to explain. Mira's question at reception is a symptom. Several causes could contribute: the Done message may leave its meaning unclear, the queue may update after she reaches reception, or a nearby sign may suggest that staff confirmation is required. Each explanation points toward a different change.

Turn the explanations into hypotheses. A hypothesis states a possible cause and predicts an observable signal. If wording causes uncertainty, Mira's explanation may focus on the message. If the queue delay causes it, her question may follow a staff screen that still shows an earlier state. A sign-related cause can be checked by observing where she looks and asking about her expectation.

Choose a discriminating check for each pair of explanations. Combine a kiosk recording, queue timestamp, and short follow-up question. The aim is to find evidence that changes the team's confidence among the explanations. A cause map keeps the symptom, candidate causes, and checks on one page.

A provisional status can still help while research continues. It can describe the receipt event and direct Mira to the waiting area, while staff use a current lookup when she asks. The final design decision follows the evidence about the main mechanism.
keyDistinction: A visible symptom can arise from interface language, system timing, or the wider setting.
workedExample: The team compares a video with logs. Mira reads Done and asks reception within 20 seconds. The service receipt arrived within three seconds, and the queue refreshed 70 seconds later. Mira says she expected reception to call her name on screen. These facts support a delayed staff view and an expectation about confirmation. The team adds a check of the lobby signage before choosing the final message.
guidedQuestion: Which next check would best separate an unclear kiosk message from a delayed staff queue?

options.label: Ask Mira what Done meant to her and compare her answer with receipt and queue timestamps.
options.feedback: This connects Mira's interpretation to the service events. The combination can guide whether the first change belongs in language, queue behavior, or both.

options.label: Review kiosk screenshots with the design team and select clearer wording.
options.feedback: A team review can generate useful wording. Include a patient explanation and the queue timing to check which part of the experience needs that wording.

options.label: Measure the average queue delay across the morning and shorten it.
options.feedback: Queue timing matters to staff visibility. Add patient observation to learn how that timing affects the meaning of the kiosk message in practice.

evidenceShift: A queue timestamp that precedes Mira's question would increase attention on wording, signage, and expectation.
transferContext: Another patient reads a wall sign saying 'Tell reception when you arrive' and then approaches the kiosk.
transferTask: Add the wall sign as a candidate influence in the cause map. Write an observation and a follow-up question that would clarify its role.
evidencePacket: Fictional observation: Mira asks reception 20 seconds after reading Done.
Fictional log: her receipt arrives three seconds after submission; the staff queue displays it 70 seconds later.
Fictional participant report: Mira expected reception to call her name on screen.
Fictional setting: one entrance sign directs arriving patients to reception.
artifact: A cause map with symptom, three hypotheses, supporting facts, and discriminating checks.
assessmentFocus: The cause map keeps observed facts distinct from explanations and selects checks that can shift the decision.
assessmentCriteria: Each hypothesis predicts an observable signal.
Every case fact has a clear evidence type.
The next checks distinguish among the candidate causes.

title: Frame a problem worth solving
outcome: Write a focused problem statement from patient and staff evidence.
context: The team has mapped the task, observed patient questions, and checked receipt and staff queue timing.
teach: A problem statement gives a team a shared account of who is affected, which task matters, what difficulty appears, and why the difficulty matters. It describes the current experience in a way that permits several possible solutions. The statement can guide further research and design discussion.

Build the statement from evidence already gathered. In this case, Mira receives a kiosk message before reception sees her arrival. During the delay she asks whether check-in succeeded. Staff spend time verifying her status. The service receipt, queue timestamp, and field note establish different parts of this sequence.

Name the consequence in terms of the task. Mira remains uncertain about her next step, and staff handle a verification request. Record the remaining uncertainty separately: the team still needs to learn how often the delay affects patients and how lobby signage shapes their expectations.

A focused statement makes the next design stage easier. It identifies an experience to improve while leaving room for message changes, queue changes, and a staff-support route. Revise the statement as the team learns more about the service.
keyDistinction: A strong problem statement describes an observed task difficulty and its consequence while leaving solution options open.
workedExample: The team writes: 'Patients who check in at the kiosk may seek staff confirmation during the interval between a service receipt and the staff queue update. This creates uncertainty about where to wait and adds verification work for reception.' They attach the field note and timestamps. They also record a research question about how often this interval produces a reception visit across different clinic sessions.
guidedQuestion: Which statement gives the design team the most useful starting frame?

options.label: The clinic needs a faster staff queue so patients can complete kiosk check-in with confidence.
options.feedback: A faster queue may help. Frame the observed uncertainty and its consequences first, then compare queue changes with other plausible responses.

options.label: Patients sometimes seek reception confirmation while kiosk and staff status differ; the team should examine the interval and its effect on waiting behavior.
options.feedback: This identifies the affected task, observed difficulty, and useful next inquiry. Add the patient and staff consequences to make the frame complete.

options.label: Patients receive a kiosk receipt before reception sees the update, and some seek confirmation during that interval, creating uncertainty and staff verification work.
options.feedback: This keeps the statement close to the supplied evidence and its consequence. The team can now explore several responses and check how often the situation occurs.

evidenceShift: Observation across quieter sessions may show a different reception pattern and narrow the problem to specific times or patient groups.
transferContext: Reception staff also report that the entrance sign directs some patients toward the desk before they reach the kiosk.
transferTask: Revise the problem statement to include the sign as a possible influence. Keep the current evidence and the next research question visible.
evidencePacket: Fictional observation: Mira asks reception for confirmation after reading Done.
Fictional log: the service receipt arrives in three seconds and the staff queue updates 70 seconds later.
Fictional operations note: reception staff answer check-in status questions during the queue interval.
Fictional setting: the entrance sign directs arriving patients to reception.
artifact: A concise problem statement with an evidence ledger and one priority research question.
assessmentFocus: The statement names the patient task, the observed difficulty, the consequence, and a meaningful uncertainty.
assessmentCriteria: The consequence includes the patient and staff experience.
The next question can refine the scope of the problem.
